A single unauthenticated `GET` request to the Directus items API can crash the Node.js process and keep it down. The
`deep` query parameter, when supplied as a JSON string, is parsed and its keys are used to build an object path that is
written with a prototype-walking setter, with no validation of the key names. A crafted payload uses inherited built-in
method names (rather than `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`) to corrupt a shared JavaScript built-in. Directus
later invokes that built-in in its logging path, which now throws outside any request handler and terminates the server.
The instance stays down until it is restarted, and the same request kills it again.

## Details

The `deep` sanitization runs inside the global query-sanitization middleware, which executes before any per-collection
permission check. A missing token is admitted as the `public` role without throwing, so the vulnerable code path is
reached by a completely unauthenticated request, and even for a collection that does not exist.

When `deep` is provided as a JSON string it is parsed and walked key-by-key into an object path, which is then written
with a setter that traverses and reuses inherited properties. Because the setter follows the prototype chain, a path
built from attacker-controlled keys named after inherited built-in methods reads the corresponding function on the
prototype and overwrites one of its properties. This corrupts a shared built-in that is used pervasively across Node.js
and Directus's logging stack. The next time that built-in is invoked (on response finalization, outside the request
try/catch), it throws an unhandled error and the process exits.

Notably:

- The write never touches `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`, so blocklists that only cover those three keys do
  not apply. Several other built-in names are reachable in the same way.
- Query-string bracket notation is not a viable delivery vector because the underlying query parser strips
  prototype-named bracket keys by default. Supplying `deep` as an opaque JSON string bypasses that protection, because
  the string is only parsed later, inside the sanitization routine, which does not strip prototype-named keys.

CWE-1321 (Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes / Prototype Pollution) leading to CWE-400
(Uncontrolled Resource Consumption / Denial of Service).

## Impact

- **Complete, persistent Denial of Service from one unauthenticated request.** The Node process exits, so the admin app
  and the entire API stay offline until an operator restarts the server.
- **Unauthenticated and pre-authorization.** The request is admitted as `public`, and the vulnerable code runs before
  any permission decision, so no public-read configuration, token, seeded data, or non-default settings are required.
- **Re-triggerable.** Process supervisors (pm2, systemd, Docker `restart: always`) bring the server back, but the same
  request kills it again, keeping the instance in a crash loop.

## References

- Fix: https://github.com/directus/directus/pull/27992
- GHSA-gwvv-rr68-cmv6

## Credits

Reported by Positive Security (https://positive.security/)
